chapter: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
title: Baton Rouge food and New Orleans as 'the city'
summary: Talk of the saloon across the street, white beans versus red beans, and how people called New Orleans simply the city.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: The big supply houses, leather finding(?) houses they'd call them, was in New Orleans. But like I said, they had a saloon in a restaurant right across the street from my house called Jim Menard's, where they had oyster loaves, chicken loaves, shrimp loaves...
Well, no, I didn't know anything about po-boy sandwiches until later in New Orleans. I can't remember anything about po-boy sandwiches in New Orleans. It was a

little different. You take red beans and rice today; that always was a New Orleans dish. In Baton Rouge, we used to like white beans, you call 'em, which is what you call navy beans. But it was cooked the same way and it was served the same way. It was cooked with ham and served with rice...
Was New Orleans a big city to the people from Baton Rouge, d'you think...
Or was it just a neighborhood...

[LAUGHS] That was the city. And every time a person was going to New Orleans, they would say, "Well, I'm going to the city." Or you'd see a guy who says, "Hey, man, where have you been?" And he didn't say, "I've been to New Orleans." Most of the time he'd say, "I've been to the city." And you'd know what they meant. And then a lot of guys said, "Well, I've been to New 'Leans." That's another pronunciation for New Orleans. And I've been to New Or-leans." Most people say "New Or-lins" now, you know.
